headings.title: Introduction to Pulmonary Circulation
headings.content: Pulmonary circulation is the vital transport network that moves blood between the heart and the lungs. Unlike systemic circulation, which supplies oxygen to the entire body, the pulmonary system exists solely to oxygenate blood and eliminate carbon dioxide. Deoxygenated blood leaves the right side of the heart, travels through the lungs where gas exchange occurs, and returns to the left side of the heart fresh with oxygen.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Pulmonary Vessels and Heart Chambers
headings.content:
The structures involved in pulmonary circulation include the right ventricle, the pulmonary trunk, pulmonary arteries, capillary beds, and pulmonary veins. 

- **Right Ventricle**: The muscular heart chamber that pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary circuit.
- **Pulmonary Trunk**: A short, wide vessel leaving the right ventricle that quickly splits into left and right branches.
- **Pulmonary Arteries**: Vessels carrying deoxygenated blood away from the heart toward the lungs.
- **Alveolar Capillaries**: A dense network of tiny vessels wrapped around the lung alveoli where gas exchange happens.
- **Pulmonary Veins**: Four vessels carrying newly oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.

headings.title: The Pathway of Blood Through the Circuit
headings.content: Blood flows in a strict sequential route through the pulmonary circuit. Deoxygenated blood is pushed out of the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the main pulmonary trunk. This trunk divides into the right and left main pulmonary arteries, heading toward each respective lung. Inside the lungs, these large arteries branch repeatedly into smaller lobar arteries, arterioles, and finally the delicate capillary beds surrounding the alveoli. After picking up oxygen, the blood collects into venules, which merge into larger pulmonary veins that empty into the left atrium.

headings.title: Gas Exchange at the Alveolar-Capillary Membrane
headings.content: The alveolar-capillary membrane is an extremely thin barrier separating air inside the alveoli from blood inside the pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses across this membrane from the alveoli into the blood, binding to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Simultaneously, carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, moving from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. This passive diffusion relies entirely on partial pressure differences between the lung alveoli and the incoming capillary blood.

headings.title: Hemodynamics and Pulmonary Blood Pressure Regulation
headings.content:
Pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system compared to systemic circulation. The right ventricle does not need to generate massive force because the lungs are close to the heart and offer low resistance to flow. 

- **Systolic Pressure**: Normally around 20 to 25 mmHg in the main pulmonary artery.
- **Diastolic Pressure**: Normally around 8 to 12 mmHg.
- **Vascular Resistance**: Pulmonary arterioles can constrict or dilate based on local oxygen levels. If an area of the lung is poorly ventilated, local vessels constrict to redirect blood to well-oxygenated areas.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Common Disorders
headings.content: Disruptions in pulmonary circulation can severely impair gas exchange and strain the heart. Conditions like pulmonary embolism occur when a blood clot travels from the deep veins of the legs and blocks a pulmonary arterial branch, causing sudden chest pain and shortness of breath. Chronic lung diseases, such as chronic bronchitis or emphysema, destroy capillary beds and increase resistance, leading to pulmonary hypertension. Over time, high pulmonary pressure forces the right ventricle to work harder, which can eventually cause right-sided heart failure, known as cor pulmonale.
